utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there's a portion of cross-examination to be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're right. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness B-1455, do you remember that the conflict in Zvornik started -- started at the same time as it did in Foca according to my information, and that is on the same day that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina took the decision to form the Territorial Defence of the republican staff? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. We can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness, there has been some trouble about the interpreters hearing you. Would you just start again, please, speaking as slowly and clearly as you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I Heard of the decision of the Presidency, and I heard that Zvornik was attacked on the 8th of April, and I heard this via the media, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was taken, if you remember, without the presence of the Serbian members of the Presidency to form the staff of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic. Have we not gone over this time and time again? What is the point of asking this witness who is from one particular municipality about who was present at a meeting of the Presidency? We waste time in this way. Now, let's move on to something else which he can deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, what is happening was happening within a context which cannot be viewed in isolation from other events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in several towns the conflict started at that time, precisely as a consequence of that decision taken by the Presidency without the Serbs. And I'm asking him whether he knows anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I am stopping you. We have witnesses who deal with all sorts of matters in a case of this sort. There will be some who no doubt can deal with that decision, but this witness is here and has given evidence about a municipality, not about the generality of politics in Bosnia at the time. And so you must confine your cross-examination to what he can deal with, and he can deal with this municipality and the evidence which he's given. Asking him generalised political questions is of no assistance to anybody, and it just wastes time. So move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I understand that the endeavours of the opposite side is to take individual incidents out of context and then to place them within a distorted picture. I understand that. But I will reduce my questions to what was happening over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that the immediate cause of the conflict in Zvornik was the mobilisation of the Muslim militia ordered by the president of the municipality and the SDA representative Avdula Pasic, a former dentist, and Nedzed Sabic, commander of the Territorial Defence who later became commander of the Podrinje Brigade of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I heard of those people from others, but that that was the cause of the conflict in Zvornik, that is the formation of such units, I don't know anything about that. I was an ordinary citizen who was endeavouring to survive together with his family, and I was not at all interested in politics. I was never a member of any party, in fact, never. And that that was the reason is something I don't know, and there's nothing I can say in answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about the events at the end of May, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that in mid-April there was an attack by Muslim extremists against the village of Rastosnica in your own municipality when the inhabitants of that village were killed? It's a Serb village. So this was more than a month prior to the events that you describe. Do you remember that? This occurred on the 17th of April, the attack on the Serbian village of Rastosnica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I was saying that that has absolutely nothing to do with why I'm here today. I heard about that, however, because I had friends in that village. And if you have information that the Muslim forces attacked that village, I don't know anything about that at all. But you do know that the aggression against Zvornik started on the 8th of April, and that that same day, within a time of 20 minutes, Zvornik was under the control of the Yugoslav army and paramilitary units. So this means that there was no resistance. There was some resistance at Kulagrad. I heard of this Rastosnica, but as to any attack and any casualties in that village, I can't tell you anything specific about that. I am here for another reason anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For another reason? Well, if you don't know anything about anything else, how is it that you say that the JNA attacked Zvornik when it didn't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people defending Kulagrad know best about that, who they had to deal with and what flag was hoisted at Kulagrad. I know from the people who deserted from that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't need to go into that any further, but as you mentioned Kulagrad, you do realise that at Kulagrad there was fighting for 20 days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that, that there was fighting at Kulagrad for 20 days, and explosions, artillery explosions could be heard as far as our village. The explosions, weapons attacking Kulagrad. And I heard that it fell on the 26th of April, and this is something I heard, and later, those men left Kulagrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know anything about the fact that in mid-April the so-called Mosque Doves, this paramilitary unit that was formed, set up road blocks on the bridges -- on the bridges across the Drina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I'm not aware of any such barricades or of any such unit. The Mosque Doves? That is something rather strange, the Mosque Doves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, since you are aware of the events in Kulagrad, do you know how the fighting evolved over 20 days? Armed groups from Kalesija and Zivinice arrived? Do you remember that? Do you remember who led them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't know anything much about the fighting there or who came there because I'm not a military person. I'm not a military analyst, nor did I live close to Kulagrad. I lived 15 kilometres away, and I know only what I heard from others, and I can't tell Their Honours something that I didn't see myself but that I just heard as rumours or information from others which need not be true, and that is why I can't talk about those things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well then. Let us be more specific and refer to some things that you mention in your statement. For instance, on page 3, paragraph 3, I'm asking you whether it is true that after the Serb forces had captured the town of Zvornik there were no particular incidents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that when the Serb forces captured Zvornik the fighting was taking place at Kulagrad for 20 days. In my village, Kostjerovo and the neighbouring village of Drinjaca, there were no incidents, no incidents, though I said after the 29th of April, after the fall of Kula, those military forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and paramilitary units came to Drinjaca and seized the weapons in the possession of the Muslims. There were no serious incidents until the 30th of May when they came and did what I described at the last hearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that same page, in paragraph 7, you say that after the 29th of April, no one went to work any more and that anyone who would try to go to work would be beaten up and sent back. That's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true. It is true. After the 29th of April, when the weapons had been seized, Major Pavlovic, who was present and who supervised the seizure of weapons in Drinjaca, gave certificates to the people who had handed in their hunting weapons with a licence. Of course, for the illegal weapons no certificates were given, no receipts were given, and he said that the weapons would be returned. And he said, "From now on, I guarantee your security. You are our loyal citizens. You are free to go back to work, be free to go shopping, to move around freely." However, when some people went to work in Karakaj - most of them were working in Karakaj, I didn't work there, I worked in Belgrade - people witnessed harassment and mistreatment, and they were returned home. I heard this from people who went there. And they went back and never returned to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. They were turned back from the barricades. And you say here that they were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They returned from those barricades. There were people who were beaten up. There were others who were mistreated and insulted without being beaten at these roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any example of somebody being beaten up? Who was beaten up? Could you give us a name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you examples because I don't remember, but I know that my brother was turned back from the roadblock. He wasn't beaten up. He was insulted. He was told to go back home and not to try and come back because nothing was working any more and there was no need for him to come. Unfortunately, he's no longer alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it possible that they didn't go to work out of fear of revenge from local Serbs because of the crimes committed before that by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, because in my village, as I said, there never was any incidents, and people were not afraid of anything because they were not guilty of anything. So we were just going to work as we were told. Some people managed to reach the factory itself, but apparently the Serbs wouldn't even exchange greetings with them there. They simply -- they -- they were told, "Can't you see it's all over? There's no work any more," and the man would just pick up his things and go back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under these circumstances that you're talking about, do you know how this is possible that no one can go to work but everybody is very peace-loving? And on the 5th of May, an attack was carried out against the village of Boskovici, the civilian population there. Again the Muslim armed formations. Nine Serb civilians were killed then on the 5th of May. Why are you representing things the other way round, that you sat at home peacefully and did nothing personally. Perhaps you did, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. Do you know anything about this attack that is alleged on this village on the 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were cut off from that part of the municipality. Boskovici is about 30 kilometres away from my village. As far as I know, some of my school friends came to school in Karakaj from those villages so I remember that. But is that moment, I did not hear where the fighting was going on. We did not receive any information. We simply still lived with the Serbs there. There were no problems. We handed in our weapons, and we barely received any information, because this territory of the south of the municipality of Zvornik was cut off when Glumina, Kulagrad, and Caparde was taken over. So no one knew what was going on on the other side of Zvornik, and I simply cannot say a thing about all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about the killing of these nine civilians on the 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I hear that? How could I know about that information, that nine civilians were killed? How could I know that? I had to listen to the Serb Radio Zvornik then. Until then, there was Radio Zvornik for everybody, for the entire population. And then there was the Serb radio Zvornik. And of course in this state of war, of course the media were in favour of the politics that prevailed in town then. So possibly something like that did take place, but I really cannot say. I mean, I can tell you what I did and what I know, but I was not there. I do not know about this, so how can I tell you anything about it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is quite logical. They expect me to know what happened in another state. That's what they expect of me here and you don't even know what happened in the municipality. Do you know the name of Semso Muminovic, Dzemal Spahic, Hajrudin Mesic, nicknamed Labud? These are people who led the extremists who were killing civilians in the villages in the municipality of Zvornik. Do you recall these names? Do you know them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about these names, but, Mr. Milosevic, they were not extremists. These were commanders of the Territorial Defence in their respective municipalities. They were defending themselves from the Serbs. They were attacked. They were shelled every day. Their women, children, civilians were being killed just as you say that people were killed in Boskovici. Well, it was the same thing. These men were our commanders of the Territorial Defence in their respective municipalities and villages. They are not extremists at all. They gave everything they could for the freedom of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I cannot accept you calling them extremists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what do you think they should be called, the people who on the 9th of May, in the attack against Gornja Baljkovica killed 16 Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's told you, Mr. Milosevic, and the argument is pointless. Your repetition of extremists is pointless. He's given you his answer. You can make your submissions to us in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I'm asking him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the defence of one's own people, one's own citizens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has told you how he characterises those people. You asked him about them, he's told you. Now move on to something else. No point arguing with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, what I'm saying is the following: If somebody comes with a group to a Serb village, kills civilians and burns the village down, do you call that defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard all this from you. But at the moment, what you're doing is examining this witness. You asked him about those people. You characterised them in some way. He denies it. He says you're wrong. Now, let's move on to something else. There's no point arguing all the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about attacks against Serb villages, Mr. May, attacks. I'm not talking about the defence of Muslim villages. I'm talking about attacks and killings of dozens of civilians, about burning these villages down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall from May 1992 attacks were launched against the village of Rozanj until they finally expelled all the Serbs from that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you keep repeating these questions to me, and I have nothing to do with these things. I lived in isolation from all of this until the 15th of July when, as a wounded person, I crossed the occupied territory, Muslim-torched villages. And then I arrived in Tuzla. It was only then that I could hear some information. But I never take information seriously unless I was present myself. I'm here to say what I saw and what happened in my local commune. I cannot testify about things that took place 30 kilometres away from where I was and where I could not go myself. Many people know this. Many people know how Muslim villages were burning, how the population was expelled, how women and girls were raped, how old men were killed, how young men were killed. Now, why would I to debate all of this here with you? In my opinion, let everybody be held accountable before this court irrespective of their ethnicity. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, everybody who committed a crime should repent and say, "This is what I did," regardless of what ethnicity they belonged to, even members of my own Bosniak people. They have to be held accountable, and I'm in favour of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is true that everybody who committed a crime should be held accountable. Everybody who committed a crime should indeed be held responsible before a legal court. Please, you are talking about something that happened in this environment, and we are trying to establish this. This happened among people who on both sides lost members of their families. You say that on the 30th of May, 1992, in Drinjaca, so that's the event that you're talking about, members of the paramilitary and soldiers of the JNA hit you, ordered you to go in front of Zaid Alic's house which is in the centre of the village, that they arrested most of the local villagers including yourself, that they were beating you, insulting you, and you say that they did not have any insignia. So is it clear that these people could not have been JNA members? The JNA have insignia. They are visible, quite visible on their sleeves, on their shoulders. So is it correct that you actually cannot confirm, and you cannot even claim that there were members of the JNA there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that they were there. I was also a member of the Yugoslav People's Army, and I know full well what kind of uniforms they wear. On the uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army while I was in the army, we had a five-pointed star that was on the cap, and on that day everybody kept their caps in their pockets, so I could not see their caps. But 100 per cent they were wearing JNA uniforms, olive-green/grey. And there were a few men there in camouflage uniform too. So this is what I claim, that this is who these people were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that everybody in the Territorial Defence from Triglav to Djevdjelija, from Slovenia to Macedonia had uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army? So what made them different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about uniforms of the JNA. Well, the entire Territorial Defence in Slovenia, Bosnia, in Croatia and Macedonia and Montenegro and Serbia, everywhere, everybody had uniforms that were the same, like the Yugoslav People's Army. But you yourself say that they did not have any insignia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that the Yugoslav People's Army, where I also did my military service, had only a five-pointed star on their caps. We did not have any insignia whatsoever in the JNA on our shoulders, none whatsoever. So of course people took off these caps. Nobody wore a cap. Hardly anybody who wore a cap then. Only those who wore black caps, those who wore camouflage uniforms. I told you about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you did your military service like I did, do you know that you did have to wear a cap with insignia if you're a member of the JNA, that those are the rules of service, that you were not allowed to take your cap off, that the cap was part of the uniform that had to be worn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did my military service in peacetime, my military service in the Yugoslav People's Army, that is, and I know when the cap can be taken off and when it cannot be taken off. But in a situation of war, was this supposed to apply to the army when there was shooting, when people were getting killed and had to get killed? So soldiers were given some liberty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what could you come to the conclusion then that these were members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said according to the olive-green/grey uniform that they were wearing, from their boots to their jackets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you anything else about this. It's -- well -- so what makes this uniform from the boots to the jacket different from Territorial Defence uniforms? Give me one single thing that makes it different.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, what makes it different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The JNA, the Territorial Defence, why are they different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any difference no difference whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm telling you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Territorial Defence and the JNA wore olive-green/grey uniforms, the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when they took you to Drinjaca, to the cultural centre there, you say that at the cultural centre you saw your armed neighbours in JNA uniforms, and you actually give their names. You give a few names here. Since you have a number here, I can give you these names, and I don't have to give you all the names. This is on page 4, paragraphs 9 and 10. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw your armed neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a few armed neighbours in uniforms of the reserve force of the Yugoslav People's Army. Some wore either trousers or something that had nothing to do with the rest, but I did see some who wore this uniform of the JNA. They were probably issued that, and they were probably helping them there get all the people together, because they cannot know our village as well as our neighbours can know it. They cannot know whose houses which ethnicity. My neighbour lived 200 metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, precisely that's what you're saying. They just wore uniforms that used to belong to the JNA. So isn't that a clear sign that they were not members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you the following: That there were many members of the reserve force of the Yugoslav People's Army who were wearing the same uniforms, olive-green/grey like my neighbours who were recruited in the reserve force. They were all mobilised, and most of them wore such uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Territorial Defence and in the army of Republika Srpska, to the best of my understanding. But then you say an officer walked into the Dom and ordered the women and children to leave. He told you that you should not be afraid, that you didn't do a thing, that you would go to see Zenica. He wore an officer's uniform, you say. He was a lieutenant, you say. Since you had done your military service, you could have established that, but then perhaps he introduced himself as a lieutenant, perhaps. And you say that he was tall, he had brown curly hair, he had an ex-JNA officer's uniform on. At the time he was about 40 years old. That's what it says here in your statement. Is it clear to you, Mr. 1455, that in the JNA there are no 40-year-old lieutenants? That can only happen in the Territorial Defence, in some kind of reserve force. But if a man were to be a lieutenant at the age of 40, he should be a lieutenant for about 15 years in order to have that rank. There is not a single lieutenant in the JNA who is that old. At the age of 40, they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This speech must end and we must come to a question. Mr. Milosevic, I should tell you that you've got something like 20 minutes left of your examination, so don't waste too much time. The point -- let the witness answer the point. The point is made that this man, at age 40, was too old to be a lieutenant. Normally if he was in the JNA, he wouldn't have been that sort of age as a lieutenant. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that that's the way he looked. And when I saw how a person looked, I mean by looking at his face. And by his face, I could infer that he was about 40. Perhaps he was between 35 and 40, but this is the way his face appeared to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Are you sure that he was not an officer of the army of Republika Srpska or some other formation there? Are you sure about that or are you not sure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not even hear of the existence of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that precisely this man at the Zvornik hospital showed this on television, this is what you say on page 5, showed a man who was killed and who was lying in a bathtub full of blood, and he said, "Look at what the Muslims did to us"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I saw on television. So I'm not trying to evade the issue. This was two or three days later. He talked about this case, that the Muslims killed this man somewhere, and again there was a caption that said "Branko Studen," a lieutenant from the garrison unit in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it say lieutenant of the unit in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The garrison in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was two or three days after the execution in Drinjaca. I'm not sure. I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it must have been June by then; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it must have been June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, as you know, there was no JNA in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the JNA left and whether it left. I wasn't really interested in that, because later on I was not a member of the army, of course. I was a disabled person, and people were protecting me in my country as a man who survived a mass execution. So I don't know, according to this information that you have, when the Yugoslav People's Army left Bosnia-Herzegovina and whether they left it at all. I don't know about this, and I cannot make any comments to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to the group of people you mentioned, the six men. Is it clear at least there that they were not members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by the uniforms, I couldn't say that they belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army because -- but judging by everything they had on them ranging from the uniforms and looking at it on television in Bijeljina, what people like that did, they looked like members of Arkan's units. But I did say that I wasn't quite sure whether they were members of Arkan's unit. Maybe that was their image, the one they liked to portray, to have uniforms of that kind, because Arkan was very famous at that time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were neither members of the JNA nor can you say with any certainty that they were members of Arkan's units either. Is that it? Because they didn't -- did they have any insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any. But I did describe the uniforms very well. And anyway, who would tell me? People here, we are members of the Arkan's units. We're killers. We instil terror and that kind of thing. Nobody Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would stand up and say that to the people around about. It's up to me to observe and conclude. So if I can't say anything, then I can't say that they were either members of the JNA or Arkan's units, although those special forces did wear uniforms that looked like Arkan's units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, different witnesses here said that there were members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards, the Zeljko Raznjatovic unit and that they had very prominent, easily visible insignia denoting that, but you say you didn't see any insignia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you hold your head down between your knees for 15 minutes and then are just given a minute or two to straighten your neck for a moment, then during that minute of fear that you experience could you really be able to differentiate who the soldiers belonged to? I was so afraid myself, and I was afraid to look at them straight in the eye. Then they might beat me up just like they beat up the other 25 people. And they were so badly beaten that they couldn't even move. They were so badly beaten. They would fall unconscious, and then they would revive them and beat them again. It was terrible to listen to these people being beaten. They would scream and cry like children and then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I understand that you weren't able to establish that, but you did notice that the commander had a beard and a moustache and all the rest of it, so I assume you don't know that not a single member of the guards had the right to wear a beard. They had to be clean-shaven and weren't allowed to wear beards, whereas you established that this man had a beard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the rules governing those units are, whether beards were regulation or not, but as he was the one who beat us most and abused us most, then it was quite normal and we were afraid of him most and we would look at him, watch him. Now, whether the rules say you can wear a beard or not, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that after that, a group of soldiers turned up with the White Eagles insignia on the caps and cockades. Now, are you aware of the fact that those weren't members of the JNA either? Is that clear? Is that point clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear to me. But don't forget that I said that there was a unit there of the JNA and those six other men who I saw there, and later on the third unit that arrived wearing Chetnik uniforms. And on some of their uniforms I saw some kinds of eagles. I couldn't look at all the soldiers, but I also saw the cockades on their caps. And of course, people like that can't be members of the Yugoslav People's Army. People know who they were. But I did specify that there were units that had no beards, that were dressed in the olive-green uniforms from head to toe except the caps, of course. It was only the fact that they did not wear any caps on their heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. We've already cleared that up. You say that your turn came and as you say the Chetniks kicked you and hit you with their rifle butts, that five many them opened fire at you and that a bullet hit you in your left hip. Is that right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sitting --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether that's correct, what I've just described as according to what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These Chetniks, the ones I saw -- yes, they were Chetniks, I saw them, of course Chetniks, and they kicked us and hit us with their rifle butts and told us to go out. And they said -- they took us to the place where they would execute us. They shot at us. And from this line-up of about six persons of this kind and once again they were not wearing caps, I don't know why, I just saw in the few seconds that I was able to see, and they shot at me and hit me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you answer fairly shortly, please, Witness 1455, because time is limited. The other point is to try and remember to watch the microphone of the accused and only answer when it's off, if you would. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So we've established that. You were hit in the left hip. And then you say that they saw that you were still alive, and then another one shot a burst of gunfire at you, and from that burst a bullet hit you in your right shoulder. From what distance did this person shoot at you? He was in front of you, I assume?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that I was hit in the left hip. It passed through my meat. I fell down, and they turned the bodies over to see if anybody was still alive. One of them kicked me in the back side and said it looks as if this one is still alive. And the other man said, "Well, what are you waiting for? Shoot another bullet at him." And then there was a burst of gunfire. They were shooting at me in my back. And on my clothing there were 11 bullet holes from under my armpit through the collar and all this, down this side. One of them hit me in the shoulder blade and exited in front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if they shot you from 1 metre distance as you say and you were hit in the shoulder; is that right? And you had 11 holes in your clothing, is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you say that after you were shot you got up and started running towards your own village and that you heard several rounds of gunfire in Drinjaca, and you were convinced that all the Muslims in the Dom had been killed, had been shot. Now, explain this to me, please: How were you able, wounded in that way, hit in the hip, and after this burst of gunfire this second time they shot at you and you say you were hit in the shoulder on that occasion, first of all, how were you able to escape without being seen if they continued these killings as you say in the Dom? How were you able to escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, fate wanted me to escape. That was my destiny. When they shot me in the back, this buffers gunfire, they said that they had run out of ammunition and then they said there were several more cases of ammunition in the Dom. But it seems to be my fate that I was able to escape and stay alive. How I managed to do that, it's very difficult for me to explain, very difficult. But as I say, the situation was such, and that was my destiny. I managed to escape. They went to get some more ammunition, and that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you were wounded in the hip and then there was this other wound that was serious in your shoulder. You managed to run and escape, to flee; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I clutched my arm to my body, and the bullet didn't hit me in the bone when it hit my hip. It was an exit/entrance wound. It went through my flesh. And as I say, I was hit in the flesh and not in the bone. Had I been hit in the bone, I probably wouldn't have been able to run away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The people who were in the Dom, in the cultural centre in Drinjaca except you, let's leave you aside for the moment because you say you didn't have any weapons, you weren't active in any way, is it possible these might have been Muslim soldiers in the Dom who had been taken prisoner during the attack launched by the Muslim forces on the villages that we mentioned? Is that possible? Or is it not possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a good question, Milosevic, the attack by Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said: Was it perhaps the Muslim soldiers that were arrested --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just deal with the question if you would. Don't get angry, because it won't help. The question is: Were there any Muslim soldiers in the Dom or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not. They were all civilians. And some of them who did have weapons, were in possession of weapons, handed them over. So they became civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were executed. All right. Now, as you've just said that and we have the records of the agency for research of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you state that when leaving the hall, you saw about 50 Chetniks holding their rifles cocked at you and that at one point Osmanvic Mehmed cried out, "Let's escape or we'll all be shot." And that you started running in different directions, and they started shooting at you. And that is page 00444845, paragraph 3. They are the minutes dated the 2nd of November, 1996, of this organisation. So they are taking you out of the Dom building as a group altogether, to send you off where they said they'd be sending you. Then this man Mehmed Osmanvic says, "Let's escape or we'll be shot," and you start dispersing and escaping, they start shooting, and some people were shot and killed. Is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to clarify my answer to you your question. When we were within two or three metres and saw the soldiers lined up, the ones who were going to shoot at us, that's when he told us to run but at the same time they ordered the soldiers to shoot and we were shot down at that very place. I don't know that anybody succeeded in escaping. What I do know was that the people in the group with me were taken out of the mass graves. Their bodies were. They were identified and given a proper burial later on. When I got up from that place, and this was for several seconds, I saw piles of dead corpses lying around me. So this was two to three metres from where the execution took place and they had already been lined up six or seven metres away from us. So I can't imagine that anybody managed to start running because they started shooting straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They started shooting when you started to run or did they start shooting -- I'm reading your statement, Witness, so I'm trying to establish what actually happened, because what you say did not happen. I don't have a single piece of evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have -- let us start again. Which page is it in the statement so the witness can understand what you're putting. I don't know if someone can give me the paragraph number. I can't see the reference to this man saying, "Let's escape." What page of the statement is it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it at page 00444845, paragraph 3. It is the minutes dated the 2nd of November, 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It sounds as though it the accused is referring to some other document, not the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe he's referring to a statement taken of the witness by the Bosnian authorities. We're seeking to get a copy of that now. It's not in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, let's not waste any more time. Yes. Now, what is the particular question you want to ask, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he described how when they went out of the hall they saw about 50 Chetniks standing round about with their rifles cocked at them, and that this man Mehmed Osmanvic shouted out, "Let's run or we'll all be killed." And this is placed in inverted commas, this "Let's run."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's take one thing at a time. Did Mehmed Osmanvic shout out as described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he did shout out, but not as he says once we'd left the hall. It was two or three metres from where the execution was to take place. That's what I said. Not as soon as we left the hall. It is true that the soldiers were there and that their numbers were the ones I had -- have quoted and that they stood right around this area below the hall, to the left of us. When we were within two or three metres of them, the casualties there, the victims where the executions had taken place, he knew that the same thing would happen to us as had happened to the previous groups, and he said, "Let's run, people, or we'll be killed. We'll die." But nobody actually started running because there was a burst of gunfire from six or seven soldiers who were shooting at us from a distance of six or seven metres. Not as we left the hall. I said precisely the way it was, and I don't want to comment on this any more because I was there, not him, and I said what happened. So we were within two or three metres of the execution site. They started shooting straight away. Now, whether somebody tried to run and escape, there was a big burst of gunfire. They started shooting at us. I didn't try to run. I just shielded my eyes and fell to the ground straight away because they were shooting at all of us, and I said that all these people were found dead in the mass graves. They didn't have a chance to escape. They were killed there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Now, time is running out. You've exceeded your time anyway, but you can ask one or two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll check what actually happened in due course, but let me just ask you this: In view of the fact that there seems to be a great deal of confusion as to the occurrence: Is this possible? Could it perhaps have been a retaliation of the inhabitants of the surrounding villages because of the crimes that had been committed earlier on and the ones I mentioned? Perhaps that is what happened, because it is impossible that somebody actually ordered an execution of the prisoners of war or civilians. So I'm trying to establish what did take place, Mr. 1455.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you this, let me put it this way, I didn't see a single neighbour of mine physically abusing people or shooting people, executing them, which means that I reject this observation that there could have been a retaliation or revenge of any kind. I said that in my area, our inter-human relations were so good that it was very rare to see such good relations prevailing anywhere else in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Our relations were very good. So I absolutely reject this idea that it could have been revenge. The plan was to kill everything that was Muslim, military-able men, and to transfer the women and children towards Tuzla, to destroy their houses, and to eradicate all trace of their ever having lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you stayed in Stanimir Mladenovic's house, a Serb, until the morning, then you continued to the village of Mijatovo across a hill where you come across some 20 Serbs from Kostjerovo wearing the uniforms of the former JNA and they were armed;, is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you came across 20 Serbs from that village. They were not members of the JNA, I assume; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they wore that kind of uniform, and also Radovan Mladjenovic who was in Drinjaca on that day. He was in the hall at the cultural centre, the Dom Kulture and I found him there among the other group. Now, whether they were neighbours, whether they actually belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the reserve force, I can't say. I don't want to enter into that system of yours, what the setup was in the army but the fact was, that they were wearing olive-green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear to me. Now, you say that you told them what happened to you, that they were shocked when they heard that the people had been killed. That's right, isn't it? At least that's what you say; right? And that they gave you something to eat. They tended to your wounds. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if they were shocked by what had happened and what you had told them, they gave you food to eat. They tended to your wound. Can you then assume that they actually took part in what happened there? Because you say that there was somebody who had been in the hall who was with them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found Radovan Mladjenovic there who was my schoolmate and one of my closest friends in my childhood up until our army days and the aggression. He was in the hall. He said, "I left before those men who were going to do what they did arrived." And he said, "I'm so sorry, neighbour, as to what happened and the condition you're in, but I left before all that happened." And of course they gave me food, and I'm grateful to them. And they dressed my wounds. But in the end I paid a very heavy price for all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to hurry because my cross-examination will be stopped. You said that Milan Ignjatovic, known as Mico, a Serb, approached you and sat next to you and said, "Don't be afraid, I'll take you to Paljevici and 1 kilometre before Paljevici he cocked his rifle behind his back you heard it and then you started running. He shot. He opened fire. He was a metre behind you. Surely it is clear that he didn't intend to kill you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me give you this answer: He did accompany me, but I always went two or three steps in front of him. And he carried a rifle, and he said that he would see me off to the Muslim village of Paljevici which still hadn't been occupied. And when we arrived about a kilometre from that village, there were meadows, and as I was walking, I was looking at the village in front of me. He stopped behind me. He was about seven or eight metres behind. He cocked my rifle. Out of fear I screamed? I said, "No, Mico." He was ready to shoot. I lay down. He opened fire, and he opened fire at me. If he had intended to do me a favour as a neighbour, he could have said, "I've been given an order to kill you because you are a witness of that execution. I will fire into the air, and you run." He could have said that. That is what he should have told me rather than chasing me around through the woods. And wounded as I was, I ran. I acquired some sort of unbelievable strength, because I was fighting for my life. And that is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could he tell you that he had received orders to kill you if he hadn't received such an order? And how is it that he wanted to kill you if he didn't shoot at you? Or did he shoot at you and miss all those times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did shoot several times, but he missed each time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question, Mr. Milosevic. You're well over time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have several more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that Murat Sabanovic and Alija Ahmetovic were killed in the village of Kostjerovo and Muriz Zahirovic in Soptonik. So they were not killed in the Dom, were they? This is on page 7, paragraph 9. So they were not killed at the cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. They were not killed there. I said that they were killed on that day resisting, according to information of some people who were watching from the woods, who resisted arrest. They were shooting at them to stop, stop. They ran. They opened fire, and they killed them. And those men were found several days later where they were killed, and they were buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a statement for TV Sarajevo, you said that the only people who arrived were Dautovic and Hasan Alic. And now giving a statement to the opposite side, in the list of those killed you said that that same Hasan Alic was killed under number 14, when were you telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is his grandfather. Hasan Alic is his grandfather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time. Yes. Let the witness continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that on the list there are two men with the same name, Hasan Alic. He was the grandfather. And there was a grandson whose name was also Hasan. It is customary in our parts for the father to give his son the name of his father. So there may be an understanding -- misunderstanding. There's Hasan Alic, the grandfather and Hasan Alic, the grandson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is going to be your last question. You're well over time, ten minutes. So ask your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to specify this point: In your statement to the opposite side, you gave the names of those killed, but in your statement to the aid agency in BH, you say that you know the names, first and last names, of people killed only from Kostjerovo, whereas the list of the others was received by you from someone else. So that is not your own knowledge but somebody else's knowledge. 00444848, second paragraph of the report dated the 2nd of November. In your statement for TV Sarajevo, you say that it was dark and that you couldn't recognise anyone. Where did you get these names from then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an answer to that question, sir. I listed most of the people from my village by their first and last names. I don't know of the actual surnames of some people from my village because it's a large village. I know people by sight. We know one another, but I wasn't really interested in their first and last names because some of them are older than me. But it is true that I listed the names of only those I was a hundred per cent sure of. As for the names of the others, I was given them by their relatives. I had to give the commission their right first and last names, and I didn't want to do any guesswork, so I got those names from their relatives and family members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Milosevic. You've had beyond your time. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for Witness B-1455, I have no questions Re-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I have just a few questions for you. How much time altogether were you in the Dom Kulture centre, from the time you were first put in there to the time you were taken out to be shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent a total of about nine to ten hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that nine to ten-hour period of time, did any member of the local Serb community come into that hall and talk about retaliation or the necessity of retaliating against those 91 men for crimes allegedly committed by Muslims? Did anybody ever address you in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the hall, there were several of our neighbours, but on no occasion did I hear any one of them say, "These people need to be shot." They didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My final question, sir, is: Would the execution of the 90 men from that hall on that day as you've described, would it have been possible without the participation of the people you have described as being members of the JNA, of Arkan's unit or Chetniks? Would it have been possible if those people were not present to participate in that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course not. I always said that we were on good terms with our neighbours, that there was no reason to do any such thing. This is confirmed by the fact that our people are returning to those villages and starting afresh. And again, they are on good terms with their neighbours. I hope you understand what I meant to say by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1455, that concludes your evidence, and you're free to go, but thank you for coming to the International Tribunal. I'm sorry you were detained over the weekend, but thank you for remaining and giving your evidence to us. Just wait until the blinds are down and then you can go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. I wish you success in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll leave the blinds down for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then may I have a couple of minutes private session before he comes in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B-1098, did you on or around the 4th of April of 1992 return from where you had been living and working to an area, part of Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at about the end of April 1992 or the beginning of May did some soldiers from Tuzla, from the Tuzla garrison of the JNA, take part in the disarming of Muslims in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they do that and what did they say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to seize the weapons and said that nothing would happen, that there would be no war, that the arms should be surrendered, that they would seize weapons from the Serbs as well. We handed in the hunting weapons we had. However, they never seized the weapons from the Serbs. They did from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldier leading this exercise came from where, did he say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldier -- this soldier was from Valjevo. I know that because when a woman handed in her husband's pistol, her husband was working in Germany, and she said, "What am I going to do now? I have no pistol and no husband." And he said, "Come to me with Valjevo and you'll be fine."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Valjevo is in Serbia. On the 29th of May, 1992, did you receive a warning? If so, from whom and to what effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Allegedly some paramilitary units had come close to our villages and that it was better for all of us to be in Klisa, all of us from these 13 Muslim villages, to gather there, and that is what happened. And this was conveyed by Vlado to an uncle of mine, and that is how we all gathered in Klisa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that stage, did you see military formations in the surrounding hills?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see what sort of military formations they were or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite sincere, I couldn't because it was far away. But you could see them over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice a car passing through a village with men in military uniform? If so, tell us about the uniforms and about the sign on the side of the car.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vehicle had the marking of the CPO, and the uniforms were SMB, olive-grey in colour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those of you gathering in Klisa sent a message by the Serbs as to what you should do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Klisa, we were promised that the UNHCR and the Red Cross would come, and I don't know which other international organisations, and that those same people would be escorted in the direction of the village of Medjedje, which is in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I stand that on tab 2, Medjedje is either the place marked as Medjedje on the left of the highlighted part of the map pretty well immediately to the left of centre slightly above Klisa but to the left nearly at the extremity of the map. "Mededa," as it reads.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B-1098, on the 1st of June, what did you discover about the village where you were all gathered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We expected the Red Cross to come and the international community. However, the army wearing SMB uniforms, camouflage uniforms, and some troops even had masks on their heads, they were there and they started shooting into the air in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly how many people as refugees were there now in this otherwise very small village of Klisa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 4.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From -- you've described the uniforms that you saw. From those uniforms, what were you able to infer as to the units represented at this operation at Klisa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by their uniforms, they were members of the JNA, the local Serbs, and I don't know who else it could have been because they wore masks over their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the crossroad at Klisa, what armament did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a crossroads I saw two tanks standing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The tanks being tanks of which force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How well or otherwise were the soldiers armed and with what sorts of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had automatic rifles. They had light machine-guns. Some of them had hand-held rocket launchers, Zoljas and Osas as we call them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any paramilitary insignia on any of the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any. I didn't really have time to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After these forces shot in the air, what were you obliged or what did other people do and then what were you all obliged to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us, people who were in their houses came out in the street, and we were shepherded towards the crossroads where the two tanks were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what did the soldiers compel you all to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then they started searching. First we had to leave our cars, because we were told we could take our tractors, our farming equipment because the UNHCR would take care of us. But all that had to be left behind. We just were able to carry our bags. However, even those bags were searched there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which direction were you compelled to move?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were moving from Klisa towards Djulici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the 4.000 at Klisa, how many were compelled to go on that route, all or any sum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How well supervised and guarded were you on that journey and how long was the journey?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went along the road, and they went on either side of the road holding their weapons, and this took about an hour or two until we reached Djulici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've spoken of the two tanks at the crossroads. Did you see anything of those tanks or other tanks along the road to Djulici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The place where you were searched, what armaments were present there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 11, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, whether in or outside your sight, to your knowledge was anybody killed on the way between Klisa and Djulici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard later that two persons had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you get to a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a new topic, paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now. Witness B-1098, we're going to adjourn for 20 minutes. Could you remember in this and any other adjournment there may be in your evidence not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn now, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B-1098, when you reached Djulici, what did you see by way of forces there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in Djulici, we saw uniformed men, men wearing camouflage uniforms, men wearing uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army, police uniforms, and some men also wore masks on their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your inference as to who the people were wearing masks was what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, they wore masks. They wore masks. I think that they were local Serbs, because if their faces were revealed, then we'd know who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although our map doesn't show it, is there another village Bijeli Potok close to and effectively connected to the village of Djulici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is connected to the village of Djulici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you all gathered together in the area between Djulici and Bijeli Potok where the men were separated from the women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as the column was coming in from the village of Klisa as we were arriving to the road by Djulici, we were ordered to raise our hands, and then we were taken to the trucks in two columns, and then they separated old men, women, and children onto a meadow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other men, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were ordered into trucks, from 16 onwards. They even included a man who was 70 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I come to what happened to the men who were boarded onto the trucks, paragraph 15 of the summary, can you help us please in brief with what happened to the villages? First of all, were at least four villages, Djulici, Luga, Setici and Klisa amongst the places that had been evacuated? Just yes or no to that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't only evacuated from these villages, there were 13 Muslim villages there that were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So far as the homes in two of those villages, I think Setici and Klisa, were the homes actually destroyed, whereas in other villages, for example, in Djulici and Luga, which doesn't show up on our map but it shows up under another name, I'll come to that, in those other villages, Djulici and Luga, were the homes left intact so that Serbs could move into them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single house was touched in Djulici. The -- whereas in the other villages they were destroyed, but in the yet remaining villages that have a Serb population only, nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that what the witness might refer to as Luga is marked as Lupici on the map slightly south-east of Djulici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B-1098, in Djulici, were homes of Muslims occupied by Serbs from a particular village in Zivinice, and if so, can you give us the name of that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djulici, Rakoda, Lupici, Mrkodo, Musici, this is where people from Brnci near Zivinice moved in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I move to paragraph 16. The men who were boarded onto the trucks which I think had been parked in Bijeli Potok, on your way to those trucks, were there further searches of the men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took away my passport and also my foreign exchange bank account book.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the second sentence. The interpreters did not manage to catch it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you repeat, please, the second sentence there. You say they took away your passport and your foreign exchange book, foreign exchange bank account book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was there anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at that moment, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many trucks, how many packed were the men on those trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw three trucks, and I think that all the men were packed into these three trucks like sardines. And there was a soldier up on top of the truck, and then he was hitting the truck so that as many men as possible would board onto the truck, and they were packed like sardines so that they wouldn't jump off the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the trucks then drive in the direction of Karakaj? If so, at what speed did they drive and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trucks took us in the direction of Karakaj. They went as fast as they could. I think that this was done in order to prevent anyone from jumping off the truck, and if the speed was that extreme, then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall now what uniforms were worn by the soldiers involved in packing these trucks and guarding them as they were guarded on the way to Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said awhile ago that they wore uniforms that were olive-grey and that they had masks on their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Karakaj --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they also had camouflage uniforms some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Karakaj did the trucks stop outside the Karakaj Technical School?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, tab 3. The Court will see by noticing the road on the left-hand side marking Bijeljina to the bottom and Zvornik to the top that the map is not orientated north/south but south/north. The version that Your Honours have because of what appears in the bottom right-hand corner should be under seal. The version being displayed on the sanction system is a redacted version that doesn't contain those details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at this map, B-1098, did the -- doesn't much matter precisely where, but did the trucks stop on the road from -- on the Bijeljina-Zvornik road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They turned a bit to the left from the road to Zvornik. There was a supermarket there before. I don't know whether it still exists. And then there's this other road that leads in a different direction. It is shown here on this sketch though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to the men in the trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They ordered the men to jump off the trucks. There were soldiers lined up there. They wore all kinds of uniforms, and they said where we were allowed to move. And this also shows the door to the hall that they forced us into. While men were jumping off the trucks, they tried to escape as much as possible the blows that these soldiers were administering to the men, but then the old men had a pretty rough time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there some Serb women in the area? If so, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were on the left-hand side of the Zvornik road, and they were shouting, "Get the balijas. Kill the balijas."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The plan, the redacted plan, tab 3, on your screen shows the technical school building into which -- or the hangar into which you were all driven. First of all, roughly how many men were forced into this building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All 700. All the approximately 700 people who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The plan here drawn by you shows the hangar in three rooms, from the left room 3, to the right room 1, and above it room 2. Taking matters shortly, was there initially a screen, an iron sheet of a screen between rooms 2 and room 1? Were you all introduced first into room 1? Did you break the screen down, some of you, in order to make more space available so that room 2 could also be used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it was. And we did manage to break it down. And that's when we managed to get some water so that we could have some water to drink.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There being water available in room 2 only, I think; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in room number 2. That's the only place where there was water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not in a position, of course, to name all 700-odd men, but you were in a position to name a number of people known to you who were included in those within the hangar. Have you signed a list which will become Exhibit 456, tab 7, I think, under seal if Your Honour pleases, and does this list which you looked at and signed this morning contain the names of some people, 39, I think, who were included with you in those rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. It does contain the names of all these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend five days in the hangar, from the 1st to the 5th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, five days we spent there. I spent five days there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the first night, did people die just simply from suffocation because they were crammed into a space too small and because, among other things, the weather was extremely hot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first day when we got there, they locked us up. I even had the impression that they turned the heating on. It was just so hot. And that's when we broke the tin sheet down, and we had some water to drink. And then in the morning when they were transferring us to yet another room, I saw that about 20 men were lying there dead, which means that they all died from the heat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you have the names of two men who you believe died from the heat. If so, can you give us the names just of the two men who died? Paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hrustan Avdic and Nesad Hamzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were given these names by someone else. I'm not going to ask you the name of the person who gave you those names. You're in a position to help further perhaps in private session if anybody needs that assistance. Paragraph 26. On the second -- on the second day, the first morning after your arrival at this hangar, were you moved from room 2 into the room on the left, room 3, and in that movement did you have to pass a desk that you've marked on the plan as "interrogation desk"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning they transferred us from room 1 to room 3. That's where there was a desk near the door, and the rest had lined up there. And as people would go out, then they would stop by the desk and then they'd ask you whether you handed in all your money, documents, your gold, your jewellery. And now when they asked me personally, I said, "You took away everything I had." He jumped up. He wanted to hit me. I managed to dodge the blow though. However, another one hit me in the back and then threw me back in line. They were hitting us with sticks. They were hitting us with truncheons, all sorts of things. When they saw that I was semiconscious, then they pushed me into the room that is marked as room A here. And I think that the rest fared more or less the same way I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness is, I think, referring to the position marked --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness is referring to the position marked A in the bottom left-hand portion of room 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B-1098, I'm sorry if it may seem repetitive, but we need to know this from time to time, the guards who were conducting the interrogation, who were taking the property and who were beating people as they moved into room 3, how were they dressed, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms. I noticed one in olive-grey too. But believe me, I didn't really have time to look at them.
